Alloy 454 is a nickel-base superalloy single crystal used for advanced jet engine turbine blades and vanes.
The gamma-prime phase volumetric content of both Alloy 454 and Mar-M 247 was near 60%.
Alloy 454 showed a greater creep rupture strength than the reference alloys Mar-M 200 and Mar-M 247.
At 760°C, orientations near the -111 to 011 axis boundary in Alloy 454 exhibited low tensile strength, with anisotropy of up to approximately 3/4 of those near the 001 axis.
Alloy 454 showed a larger allowance in high creep strength off-axial orientation from the 001 axis, and relatively poor creep strength near the -111 axis, compared to other superalloys.

TEM observations showed that the regular arrangement and form of the gamma-prime phase was entirely disintegrated in the -111 orientation, while the gamma-prime phase retained its cubic geometric shape and arrangement in the 001 and 011 orientations.

The anisotropic behavior of Alloy 454 was explained in terms of the available slip systems and the stacking geometry of the gamma-prime precipitates, which are well-hardened by the large tantalum content.
Alloy 454 was solution treated at 1280°C for 4 hours and aged at 871°C for 32 hours.
The tensile axis orientations of the samples used in the study were determined using Laue's reverse X-ray method.
Tensile testing was performed at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 1000°C, and creep testing was performed at temperatures ranging from 760°C to 1000°C.
Creep testing was performed at stress levels of 77.3 kgf/mm^2 (760 MPa) at 760°C and 20.5 kgf/mm^2 (200 MPa) at 982°C.
The distribution of the tensile axis orientations of the samples used in the orientation dependency testing was plotted on standard stereographic triangles.
After testing, representative samples were sliced and observed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to study the dislocation structures.
The Schmid factor contours for the most highly stressed slip systems were plotted on standard stereographic triangles to help explain the anisotropic behavior.

The anisotropic behavior of Alloy 454 was attributed to the high degree of precipitation hardening of the gamma-prime phase, which made the $111<112> slip system less active compared to other superalloys.
